summary: לֹא (lo) negates a verb, an adjective, an adverb or a whole predicate and stands directly before it: הוּא לֹא אוֹהֵב חֲצִילִים, הַבָּצָל לֹא פֹּה. In the present tense, “there isn’t / I don’t have” is אֵין (the opposite of יֵשׁ): אֵין לִי גֶּזֶר. Prohibitions use אַל + future (אַל תִּקְנֶה!). The answer “no” is also לֹא.

askYourself: Is it “there is no …” or “… doesn’t have …” in the present? → אֵין (never *לֹא יֵשׁ).
Is it a past or future possession/existence? → לֹא הָיָה / לֹא יִהְיֶה.
Otherwise: put לֹא immediately before the verb, adjective or predicate.
Is it a command not to do something? → אַל + future.
Is there a negative word like כְּלוּם (nothing)? → you still need לֹא.

traps: *לֹא יֵשׁ is wrong — say אֵין: אֵין לִי זְמַן.
לֹא goes before the verb, not after it: הִיא לֹא אוֹכֶלֶת.
Double negation is normal: אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם.
The answer “no” and the negation “not” are the same word: לֹא, אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה.
אֵין negates only the present; for the past use לֹא הָיָה / לֹא הָיְתָה.

seeAlso.note: Arabic chooses its “not” by tense and type (لَا, لَمْ, لَنْ, لَيْسَ, مَا); Hebrew mostly needs לֹא, with אֵין for “there isn’t”.
German splits nicht and kein (no + noun); Hebrew uses לֹא for both.
Chinese splits 不 (general, present, future) from 没 (have not, did not); compare Hebrew לֹא vs אֵין.
